{{1998 Winter Olympics}}

[[File:1998 Winter Olympics medals.JPG|thumb|The silver, gold, and bronze medals|alt=Three round medals with blue ribbons hanging in a display. The medals are silver, gold, and bronze from left to right.]]

The [[1998 Winter Olympics]], officially known as the XVIII Olympic Winter Games, were a winter [[multi-sport event]] held in [[Nagano, Nagano|Nagano]], Japan, from 7 to 22 February 1998.<ref>{{cite book|author=((The Organizing Committee for the XVIII Olympic Winter Games, Nagano 1998))|title=The XVIII Olympic Winter Games Official Report – Volume I|publisher=[[LA84 Foundation]]|year=1998|location=[[Nagano, Nagano|Nagano]], Japan|url=http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/1998/Vol1_e.pdf|access-date=5 June 2024|archive-date=6 May 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100506004809/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/1998/Vol1_e.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Twenty-four nations earned medals at these Games, and fifteen won at least one gold medal; forty-eight countries left the Olympics without winning a medal. Competitors from [[Germany at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Germany]] earned the highest number of gold medals (12) and the most overall medals (29). With 10 gold medals and 25 overall medals, [[Norway at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Norway]] finished second in both categories.<ref name="individual"/> [[Denmark at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Denmark]] won its first Winter Olympics medal,<ref>{{cite news | last = Chase | first = Chris | title = The USA hasn't won the Winter Olympic medal count in 86 years (and 21 other crazy Olympic facts) | work = [[USA Today]] | date = 2 February 2018 | url = https://olympicswire.usatoday.com/2018/02/02/usa-winter-olympic-medal-count-won-86-years-facts-winter-pyeonchang-stats/ | access-date = 14 April 2018 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180212083316/https://olympicswire.usatoday.com/2018/02/02/usa-winter-olympic-medal-count-won-86-years-facts-winter-pyeonchang-stats/ | archive-date = 12 February 2018 }}</ref> while [[Bulgaria at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Bulgaria]] and the [[Czech Republic at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Czech Republic]] won their first Winter Games gold medals.<ref>{{cite web | title = The big chill: Heavy snow shuffles schedule; luger wins third gold | publisher = CNN Sports Illustrated | date = 9 February 1998 | url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/olympics/events/1998/nagano/news/1998/02/09/roundup/ | access-date = 16 March 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629122806/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/olympics/events/1998/nagano/news/1998/02/09/roundup/|archive-date=29 June 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | last = Druzin | first = Randi | title = The XVIII Winter Games: Ice Hockey; In Prague, 70,000 Fans Gather to Savor Moment | work = [[The New York Times]] | date = 23 February 1998 | url = http://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F00815FF3C5A0C708EDDAB0894D0494D81 | access-date = 29 December 2010 }}</ref> [[Azerbaijan at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Azerbaijan]], [[Kenya at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Kenya]], [[Macedonia at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Macedonia]], [[Uruguay at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Uruguay]], and [[Venezuela at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Venezuela]] competed for the first time, but none of them won a medal.<ref name="IOC"/>

Varying statistics are reported for the number of participants at the 1998 Winter Olympics. The [[Sports Reference|Sports-Reference]] website states that 2,180 athletes from 72 nations participated in 68 events from 14 [[Olympic sports#Winter Olympics|sports and disciplines]].<ref name="individual"/> Olympic historian [[Bill Mallon]], in his ''Historical Dictionary of the Olympic Movement'', agrees with the figure of 2,180 participants.<ref>Mallon and Heijmans, p. 407.</ref> In contrast, the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) website reports that 2,176 athletes competed at the Games.<ref name="IOC"/> The sport of [[Curling at the 1998 Winter Olympics|curling]] returned after a single appearance in the [[Curling at the 1924 Winter Olympics|1924 Olympics]], [[Snowboarding at the 1998 Winter Olympics|snowboarding]] was added as a new sport, and [[Ice hockey at the 1998 Winter Olympics|women's ice hockey]] made its first appearance in the Olympics.<ref name="IOC">{{cite web | title = Nagano 1998 | publisher = International Olympic Committee | url = http://www.olympic.org/nagano-1998-winter-olympics | access-date = 5 June 2024 | archive-date = 2 June 2011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110602015834/http://www.olympic.org/nagano-1998-winter-olympics | url-status = live }}</ref> 

The leading medal winner at the Games was [[Russia at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Russian]] skier [[Larisa Lazutina]], who won five medals, including three golds.<ref name="individual">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=1998 Nagano Winter Games   |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1998/ |access-date=19 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090425191343/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1998/ |archive-date=25 April 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The only other athlete to win three gold medals was Norwegian skier [[Bjørn Dæhlie]], who won four medals overall, making him the first Winter Olympian to win twelve career medals, eight of which were gold.<ref name="individual"/><ref name="Dahlie">{{cite news |title=Dahlie claims 12th medal; Czechs take hockey gold |agency=[[Associated Press]] |work=[[Amarillo Globe-News]] |date=23 February 1998 |url=http://amarillo.com/stories/022398/LS0165.001.shtml |access-date=9 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604040445/http://amarillo.com/stories/022398/ls0165.001.shtml |archive-date=4 June 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Nine other athletes won three medals, including three Germans.<ref name="individual"/> [[United States at the 1998 Winter Olympics|American]] [[Figure skating at the 1998 Winter Olympics|figure skater]] [[Tara Lipinski]] became the youngest competitor in Winter Olympics history to earn a gold medal in an individual event.<ref name="IOC"/>

==Medal table==
{{see also|Olympic medal table}}
[[File:HMaier2.jpg|thumb|right|[[Austria at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Austrian]] skier [[Hermann Maier]] won gold medals in the Super G and Giant Slalom.<ref>{{cite news | last = Clarey | first = Christopher | title = Two Gold, One Stunning Crash: Now Maier Is Fast and Familiar | work = The New York Times | date = 20 February 1998 | url = https://www.nytimes.com/specials/olympics/nagano/ski/022098oly-ski-maier.html | access-date = 17 March 2009 }}</ref>|alt=A man wearing a black shirt and hat.]]
[[File:Nagano 1998-Russia vs Czech Republic.jpg|right|thumb|The men's [[Ice hockey at the 1998 Winter Olympics|ice hockey]] gold medal game between Russia and the Czech Republic|alt=A hockey game between two teams; one is wearing red uniforms, and the other has white jerseys, red pants, and blue helmets.]]
[[File:Claudia Pechstein 2008.jpg|thumb|right|German [[Speed skating at the 1998 Winter Olympics|speed skater]] [[Claudia Pechstein]] won a gold medal in the women's 5,000 meters and a silver in the 3,000 meters.<ref>{{cite news|last=Newberry |first=Paul |title=Teammate Grabs Gold From Niemann-Stirnemann |agency=Associated Press |work=[[The Washington Post]] |date=20 February 1998 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/sports/longterm/olympics1998/sport/speedsk/articles/olyspeed20.htm |access-date=17 March 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121108031958/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/sports/longterm/olympics1998/sport/speedsk/articles/olyspeed20.htm |archive-date=8 November 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>|alt=A female speed skater turns around a curve. She is wearing a black and blue body suit.]]

The medal table is based on information provided by the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) and is consistent with IOC conventional sorting in its published medal tables. The table uses the [[Olympic medal table]] sorting method. By default, the table is ordered by the number of gold medals the athletes from a nation have won, where a nation is an entity represented by a NOC. The number of silver medals is taken into consideration next and then the number of bronze medals.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ostlere |first1=Lawrence |date=11 August 2024 |title=Olympic medal table: USA beat China to top spot at Paris 2024 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2580716.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240812015233/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2594580.html |archive-date=12 August 2024 |access-date=12 August 2024 |work=[[The Independent]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Araton |first1=Harvey |date=18 August 2008 |title=A Medal Count That Adds Up To Little |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321004238/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |archive-date=21 March 2023 |access-date=25 July 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> If teams are still tied, equal ranking is given and they are listed alphabetically by their [[List of IOC country codes|IOC country code]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cons |first1=Roddy |date=10 August 2024 |title=What happens if two countries are tied in the Olympic medal table? Tiebreaker rules explained |url=https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240811152350/https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |archive-date=11 August 2024 |access-date=11 August 2024 |work=[[Diario AS]] |language=en-us}}</ref>

In the [[Bobsleigh at the 1998 Winter Olympics#Two-man|two-man bobsleigh]] competition, a tie meant that two gold medals were awarded, so no silver medal was awarded for that event.<ref>{{cite web | title = Highs and lows: Japanese jumpers soar; Canadian curlers fumble gold | publisher = CNN Sports Illustrated | date = 23 February 1998 | url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/olympics/events/1998/nagano/news/1998/02/15/roundup/ | access-date = 14 March 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629122529/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/olympics/events/1998/nagano/news/1998/02/15/roundup/|archive-date=29 June 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> A tie for second in the [[Alpine skiing at the 1998 Winter Olympics|men's Super G skiing]] competition meant that a pair of silver medals were given out, so no bronze medal was awarded for that event.<ref>{{cite news | last = Clarey | first = Christopher | title = The XVIII Winter Games: Alpine Skiing; Three Days After Spectacular Crash, Maier Wins Gold | work = The New York Times | date = 16 February 1998 | url = https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D0CE1DE163FF935A25751C0A96E958260 | access-date = 15 March 2009 }}</ref> In the [[Bobsleigh at the 1998 Winter Olympics#Four-man|four-man bobsleigh]], a tie for third resulted in the awarding of two bronze medals.<ref>{{cite news|last=Olson |first=Lisa |author-link=Lisa Olson |title=Tough Sledding As Medal Slips, U.S. Hits Skids |work=[[Daily News (New York)|New York Daily News]] |date=22 February 1998 |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/1998/02/22/1998-02-22_tough_sledding____as_medal_s.html |access-date=9 July 2019 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20090513185058/http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/1998/02/22/1998-02-22_tough_sledding____as_medal_s.html |archive-date=13 May 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Due to these ties, the number of gold medals awarded was one more than the number of silver or bronze medals. In [[Snowboarding at the 1998 Winter Olympics|snowboarding]], [[Canada at the 1998 Winter Olympics|Canadian]] [[Ross Rebagliati]] won the gold medal in the men's Giant Slalom, but it was briefly stripped by the IOC after he tested positive for marijuana. After the Canadian Olympic Association filed an appeal, however, the IOC's decision was overturned.<ref>{{cite web |last=Gross |first=George |author-link=George Gross (journalist) |title=Ross Rebagliati: 1998 – Nagano, Japan |work=[[Sun Media Corporation]] |publisher=[[Canadian Online Explorer]] |date=21 February 2006 |url=http://slam.canoe.com/Slam/Olympics/2006Turin/MomentsOfGlory/2006/02/14/pf-1442844.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002005914/http://slam.canoe.com/Slam/Olympics/2006Turin/MomentsOfGlory/2006/02/14/pf-1442844.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2 October 2015 |access-date=22 April 2026 }}</ref>
